text: The assembly will hear an address by his
excellency Al Anthony Albanesei, Prime
Minister of the Commonwealth of
Australia. I request protocol to escort
his excellency and invite him to address
the assembly.
My dear colleagues, this evening I want
to talk about the need for nations to
work together on the new challenges that
we face. Climate change, emerging
technology, and the breakdown of
international rules. Eight decades ago,
the citizens and leaders of our nations
made a solemn promise to future
generations.
Having known the untold sorrow of two
devastating global conflicts in their
lifetimes, they vowed to work together
to prevent another. The pioneers who
built this institution from the ruins of
war, proud Australians among them, were
also coming to terms with two terrible
truths. The horrors of the Holocaust and
the unprecedented horror of nuclear
weapons, a depth of evil and a scale of
destruction beyond imagining even a
decade earlier. Yet rather than recoil
from that reality, our leaders stood
together to face it, learn from it, and
most importantly, guard against its
return. And instead of surrendering to
fear or dealing in retribution or
abandoning their fate to a world
governed by force alone, they came
together to renew and affirm their faith
in humanity, in the essential and equal
dignity and worth of every individual,
in the sovereignty of every nation, and
in the capacity and indeed the
responsibility
of all of us to give the Universal
Declaration of Human Rights life and
weight and real meaning by engaging in
the dialogue that builds trust and
deepens understanding and backing those
words with actions.
In this moment, we need to lean in and
strengthen and modernize the fundamental
parts of the UN system that help to
build peace and promote economic
development and sustainability.
Sovereignty, prosperity, and peace are
never guaranteed. They must be created,
nurtured, and protected by each
generation supporting the jobs, homes,
schools, and health care that represent
the fullest expression of the UN's
commitment to the economic and social
advancement of all peoples. We know that
the shest way to minimize the potential
for conflict is to create the
prosperity, opportunity, and economic
justice on which lasting peace depends.
That means cooperating on the urgent
challenge that confront each of our
sovereign nations and creating solutions
that work for our citizens. This was the
founding purpose of the United Nations.
And for the leaders who have gathered
here this week, this remains the test of
our time. A test we can and we must
pass. Whether it is climate change or
artificial intelligence, there is always
the temptation to say that our
generation is being confronted by issues
that our predecessors could not possibly
have imagined. While dealing with the
world they would not recognize.
But for all the transformation the past
eight decades have brought, the fund
fundamental stakes haven't changed. And
just as its values, our values, our
ideals, our commitment to dialogue and
cooperation proved equal to that task,
then we can rise to meet these new
challenges. Now we can reaffirm our
national sovereignty and our shared
humanity. We can seize and share and
shape the opportunities this moment
holds in the interests of our citizens.
But we can only do it together. From the
very first days of this forum, Australia
has always known that. We understand
that the UN mission cannot be entrusted
solely to the great powers or the
biggest countries or even the loudest
voices alone. Nor can it be
subcontracted to the world's richest
companies or dictated by the pace of
technology.
then, now and always. Shaping a secure,
peaceful and prosperous world is a task
for all of us. And that world must be
driven by the values and aspirations of
all of us. We all have a part to play.
And that is why Australia is seeking a
non-permanent seat on the UN Security
Council for 2029
The world faces tough times and
Australia wants to respond to partner
and to make a difference. Should our
security council bid proved successful,
our purpose and approach will be
consistent with how we have always
conducted ourselves at the UN. We will
listen with respect. We will partner as
equals and we will protect what matters
most.
Mr. President, a safer world is one
governed by rules, not by power and
force alone. It is a world in which all
countries have the freedom to decide
their own future, and all countries have
their decisions listened to. As a member
of the UN Security Council, Australia
will safeguard the rules that protect us
all by upholding international law,
including the UN Charter, and the
sovereignty of all states. We will
amplify the voices of small states and
middle powers to ensure a wider range of
perspectives shape the council's
decisions. We will work to prevent
crisis, revolve, resolve conflicts and
protect civilians through diplomacy,
peaceuilding and practical action. Our
objective will be to support a more
effective, representative and responsive
UN that is equipped to address the fast
growing challenges of today. Listening,
partnering, protecting.
Colleagues, the world is changing
rapidly. New issues are becoming
international issues demanding our full
attention. Climate change where the
science foretold of the increase in
frequency and intensity of extreme
weather events that we are now
experiencing. emerging technology
including artificial intelligence which
is evolving at a furious pace and the
breakdown of trust, civility and social
cohesion which is promoting conflict
within and between countries. Clearly
the multilateral system we have all
known and benefited from is under
immense strain. To promote the peace, to
create a world of human dignity, to do
justice to the UN's mission, we must
embrace change and we must embrace
reform. Australia supports the rules and
institutions that underpin open trade
and connectivity. That order based on
agreed rules and institutions faces
massive disruption. This doesn't mean
abandoning multilateralism. It means
working to reform it so it's up to the
challenges ahead and building beyond
multilateralism with new coalitions and
partnerships to address and solve
complex problems. As a middle power,
Australia is showing leadership and
working with others on fresh ideas to
tackle the big issues now facing the
world. In our region, the Indo-Pacific,
we are elevating relationships that help
to build sovereign capability and offer
nations sovereign choice free from
coercion so that our partners can
address the big issues confronting them.
Economic security, human development,
energy security, transnational crime,
sovereign capabilities, trade and
investment, and science and technology.
Whether it's our support for our Pacific
family, our partnerships in Southeast
Asia, the elevation of our relationships
with Japan, India, and the Republic of
Korea, or the deepening of our
partnerships with Europe, and Canada.
This is our approach. We seek to amplify
the voices of small and midsize states
to ensure council decisions are informed
by the widest possible perspectives.
working strongly together on issues that
matter to us, to them, and to the world.
Listening, partnering, protecting. We
are developing these new partnerships
while continuing to work closely with
our principal ally, the United States,
and our major trading partner in China.
Australia stands for a safer world where
no country dominates and no country is
dominated. Crises are prevented,
disputes are settled through rules and
dialogue, and institutions deliver
outcomes.
There are so many issues to confront
urgently and cooperatively. Last year at
this assembly, Australian parents spoke
to world leaders about their campaign
resulting in our nation's social media
ban for under 16s. Those parents
channeled their personal grief into a
powerful call for global action and the
world has answered. Already more than 20
countries are bringing in or have
brought in age restrictions on social
media. And with the European community
taking action, there are many more to
come. More recently, our government has
announced a digital duty of care. Its
purpose is to deliver control back into
the hands of people by empowering them
to determine what appears in their feed,
giving them the choice. The
technological development that must now
be the subject of public discussion is
artificial intelligence.
AI can improve lives, boost growth and
productivity, provide revolutionary
breakthroughs in health care and other
fields. But leaders of AI companies
themselves have warned of the potential
risks to allow Frontier AI to develop
too fast without guard rails. Recently,
an artificial intelligence agent
infiltrated an Australian government
website. This is unacceptable and it is
why Australia has been leading the way
in establishing Australian standards for
AI. Standards to ensure that AI will
work and deliver for people, not the
other way around. We can't ignore AI or
prevent it. And it's why we joined with
other nations this week to call for
action to shape artificial intelligence
development rather than be passively
shaped by it.
Australia is a nation built on fairness
and opportunity that promotes equality
and respect for all people. We work to
prevent conflict, protect civilians, and
defend the rules that protect us all. We
uphold international law including the
UN charter and support bold practical
reform to ensure the UN can best fulfill
its mandate into the future. We are
strong supporters of freedom of
navigation and overflight for all
nations just as we are in our efforts to
combat nuclear proliferation.
We oppose Russia's continued, illegal,
unprovoked, and immoral invasion of
Ukraine and reiterate our calls for
Russia's immediate, complete, and
unconditional withdrawal and an end to
attacks upon civilians and civilian
infrastructure.
This week, Australia endorsed the 2026
International Crimea Platform joint
statement, reaffirming our respect for
Ukraine's sovereignty, independence,
unity, and territorial integrity within
its internationally recognized borders.
And we signed a new bilateral security
agreement with Ukraine to complement the
humanitarian and military support that
we have provided.
When countries facing disaster and
conflict reach out for help, Australians
always respond generously with
humanitarian assistance. We have a
solemn duty to protect those who
undertake this vital work. Last year,
following the killing of Australian aid
worker Zami Frankham and the deaths of
over 1,000 other humanitarian workers in
the last three years, Australia and
eight partner nations led the
development of a declaration for the
protection of humanitarian personnel.
now supported by 130 countries. That
declaration outlines practical measures
to ensure stronger accountability, safer
access, and better protection for aid
workers operating in conflict zones.
Again, listening, partnering, protecting
Australian values at work, in practice.
Colleagues, last year Australia took the
considered decision to join other
partners and recognize the state of
Palestine. It was motivated by the
determination to try and end a cycle of
violence that has stolen too many
innocent lives. We know the only viable
path to peace and security in Palestine,
in Israel, and in the broader Middle
East is through a two-state solution
where the people of Israel and the
people of Palestine can raise their
children in freedom and safety. We will
continue to speak out against actions
that damage that prospect of peace,
including illegal settlements in the
West Bank. Just as we continue to oppose
any role for the terrorists of Hamas in
Palestine's future, the conflict in Iran
has taken a severe toll on the Middle
East and has had a devastating impact on
the global economy. Australia has been
consistent in our calls for a ceasefire
and for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen
and restore the freedom of navigation
and trade. And we continue to call for
Iran to halt its indiscriminate attacks
on the region and to abandon any program
to obtain nuclear weapons.
Colleagues, Australia's approach to
diplomacy is both local and global. Our
geography gives us a unique perspective.
As a Pacific nation inhabiting an entire
continent and connected to Southeast
Asia, the Indian Ocean and Antarctica,
we feel joined to our region not just by
geography, but by our close human
connections, including family. We are
one of the world's most successful
multicultural democracies. Proudly home
to the oldest continuous civilization on
earth, our First Nations, Aboriginal and
Toouristra Islander people. And home
also to people from more than 300
different ancestries with more than half
of our population either born overseas
or having at least one parent born
overseas. We are investing in the
multilateral system by elevating Pacific
voices in shaping global decision
making, working with them to advance
their development needs and counter the
transnational organized crime that is
spreading across the beautiful Pacific
Ocean that we share and addressing
climate change which threatens their
very existence through rising sea levels
and increasing salinity. Accepting the
science of climate change and acting
upon it is rightfully the entry point
for engaging with these vital nations of
the Pacific or as we call it the blue
continent. It's why we are partnering
with the COP 31 president TIA and
Pacific nations to sponsor a Pacific
pre-COP meeting in Fiji and Tubalu.
Pacific countries have long been leaders
on climate action. Their voices are
central to shaping the global response
and we proudly work with them.
Mr. President, Australia's purpose in
its relations with the United Nations is
clear and our approach is principled. We
listen with respect. We partner as
equals and we protect what matters most.
We engage across regions, listen to
different perspectives, and we build
trust. We champion the rights,
sovereignty, and agency of all,
particularly smaller and midsize
nations. We are a reliable, practical,
and transparent partner. And we play our
part to protect the people of the world
by taking on the difficult challenges
shaping their lives and the health of
their planet with innovative ideas and
approaches. Australia helped create the
United Nations to bring an end to an era
of destructive conflict and to build
something better for all of us. A world
where prosperity is driven by shared
opportunity and peace is secured by
collective responsibility.
Australia is stepping up to play our
part. I thank you.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the prime minister of the
Commonwealth of Australia.
